s08.slug: TUESDAY · 5:15 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — CANDLEMAS
s08.music: The St. Brendan’s Choir — “Lumen ad revelationem gentium”
body: The sun is down behind the ridge, but the sky over it hasn’t got the news yet, a long bruised yellow going green at the top, and the olive-tree courtyard at St. Brendan’s is full of people holding candles that aren’t lit: Newman kids in hoodies, the weekday regulars, a nurse in scrubs and clogs straight off a shift. Joey Abruzzo has the basket at the gate and is telling everybody within a block that the paper drip guards ran out at the 12:10.

Skye’s candle is bare. She went upstairs after the call and came down in the gray cardigan, the sixty-eight-dollar one she bought for Mass, the flannel left on the swing, and now she holds the candle in front of her in both fists and studies the wick.
“What’s my motivation,” she says, low.
“Don’t set anybody’s hair on fire.”
“That’s a note. That’s not a motivation.”

Father Osei comes out the side door in white, a server behind him with a lit taper, and the flame goes out through the crowd wick to wick until the courtyard is full of small fire. He reads the blessing, short, and swings the aspergillum. The drops land cold on Jack’s cheek. Skye shuts her eyes and takes hers on the face like weather. A gust comes down off the ridge and takes a dozen flames at once, hers among them.
She turns to him without a word and tips her wick into his.

He holds still for it. Her face is lit from underneath, a loose piece of hair at her ear, her eyes crossed a little with the care she’s taking, her breath moving both flames. The wax smells like a sacristy. It takes. She doesn’t step back right away, and he wants her, here, with the holy water drying on his face, and there’s no use pretending otherwise to God, who has the better view. The woman on her other side holds out a dark wick, and Skye lights it, and the woman lights the next.

Past the fountain, Laney Price is holding her candle out at the full length of her arm, away from her hair, with the face of a woman defusing something. Lena is beside her, her own candle held close. Jack sees her the way you see anybody across a courtyard of candles, one lit face in a crowd of them, and looks past her through the open doors to the altar. Two girls from Newman look from him to the fountain and back, and find something to do with their candles when he catches them.
“Let us go in peace,” Osei says, “to meet the Lord.”

*Lumen ad revelationem gentium*, the choir sings at the doors, and the line goes in under it, out of the dusk and up the aisle under the ship’s-hull ceiling, the blue glass gone black in the windows above a churchful of candles. Halfway up, a bead of wax runs down Skye’s candle and over her thumb. Her mouth tightens. She doesn’t move the thumb. By the pew it has cooled to a white cap on the knuckle.

Osei reads the Gospel himself: Mary and Joseph bringing the child up to the Temple with two turtledoves because they can’t afford the lamb, and old Simeon taking him in his arms. *A light for revelation to the Gentiles.* Then the prophetess, Anna, a widow till she was eighty-four, who never left the temple.
Skye leans in to his ear. “Eighty-four,” she whispers. “She waited eighty-four years for an *entrance*.”
Jack has to look at his shoes until the Gospel is over.

Osei closes the book. “Simeon waited his whole life to see one thing, and when they put it in his arms he did not say, *Now I will keep him*,” he says. “He asked to be let go. And to the mother he says, *and you yourself a sword will pierce* — and the light is for the Gentiles, which is to say for everybody, which is the hard part, because everybody includes the one you would not have invited.” He goes back to his chair.

Jack thinks of Ma at the Trumbull vending machines every other Sunday with a sandwich bag of quarters, and of *Professor* on the porch this afternoon with nothing after it. At the intentions he adds his own, straight. *Twenty-three today. He’s got a book coming late. Keep him till it gets there. Keep him after.*

At Communion Gus keeps the organ low and the pews empty forward one by one from the front. When it’s theirs, Jack doesn’t stand. Skye doesn’t get up to let him by. She turns her knees to let the row out past them, and while Jack is still working out what to do with his candle she takes it out of his hand and holds it with hers, one in each fist, his and the bare one with the wax on her thumb.
He kneels. She stays sitting beside him, straight-backed, holding them both.
He says the Act of Contrition slowly, the one he could say in his sleep, and slows down more at *firmly resolve*, and gets to the end of it.

The line coming back goes down the side aisle past the end of the pew, and with his head bowed he sees it from the knee down: a toddler’s light-up sneaker, a pair of wingtips, a candle held out at the full length of somebody’s arm though it’s been out since the Gospel. Beside it, a pair of flats slows at the end of the pew and stops, longer than the line has stopped. A hand settles on the back of Laney’s coat and steers her on into a pew farther down.
Jack keeps his head down. Beside him Skye gets both candles into one hand and puts the other on his back, high up, and keeps it there till he sits.
At the door Osei has a candle in his left hand and takes Jack’s with his right, and holds it a second longer than a handshake. His eyes are having a wonderful time.
“I saw your concert,” he says.
And nothing else. He lets go, sees Skye’s full hands, and gives her a little bow from the neck instead. She bows back exactly as far.

Becca Lindell is on the step below in a peacoat with her own candle. “Happy Candlemas, Jack,” she says. “Hi, Skye.” She looks at the wax on Skye’s thumb, slides the paper guard off her own candle, and fits it down over Skye’s until it sits against the knuckle. “There,” she says.
Mrs. Fitch is at the foot of the steps, collecting stubs in Joey’s empty basket. “Mr. Costigan,” she says. “Four people have asked me whether that was you. I told them I was sure it was not.”
Skye presses her lips together until they go white and holds them that way to the bottom of the steps.

Under the olive trees people are carrying their candles off to the lot, the flames out, the wax still soft. Skye hands Jack back his candle. She looks at the two of them, his and hers, Becca’s guard very white on hers.
“I held those through the good part,” she says. “I want that in the credits.”

response: He holds his out to her. She looks at it, and at him, and takes it, and gives him hers straight back.
“Trade,” she says. “Then we’ve both got one the other one held.”
He puts hers in the inside pocket of the Carhartt, Becca’s guard and all. She carries his across the lot to the Saab and lays it on the dash like a corsage, and tells it to stay.
“For Nonna,” he says. He’ll tell her about it on the phone: candles lit outdoors in February under olive trees, a priest from Ghana with holy water, a gust. You can’t mail fire.
Skye nods like that’s obviously correct, and carries hers down the walk to the lot in both hands, like it’s still lit.
